agent_1.question: How is the surplus that exceeds the 200 kg community catch cap redistributed or returned to the lake, and who is responsible for deciding and enforcing that distribution?
agent_1.answer: In practice we keep the lake’s stocks healthy by making sure any amount that pushes the community’s total over the 200 kg cap is put back into the water.  Each fisher tallies their haul and sends it to the community board.  The steward—who is the fisher that logs the most accurate totals that day, rotating among us—adds all the numbers.  If the sum is more than 200 kg the surplus is first taken off the books:  if the extra weight is still in a fisher’s boat, that fisher must set it back into the lake before heading home.  If any of the excess has already been taken, we divide the remaining surplus equally among all participants who took a haul that day and give each fisher that portion of the next trip’s catch (a small bonus).  The steward then records the split and informs everyone.  Anyone who fails to report or deliberately overfishes is fined by giving up 2 kg on the next trip, and the steward enforces that penalty.  The steward’s role is to tally, verify, decide how surplus is handled, and enforce the penalties.  This keeps the lake stocked and our community fair.

agent_2.question: Who will be responsible for enforcing the temporary fishing moratorium and for collecting and holding the fines that fishers pay into the community pot?
agent_2.answer: We will form a Lake Steward Committee made up of experienced fishers who rotate responsibility every quarter. They will enforce any temporary moratorium. The communal ledger keeper will collect the 1 kg fines, keep them in the community pot, and report the balances each month.
agent_2.revised_policy: Each fisher may take no more than 15 kg per trip, and only fish larger than 20 cm may be kept. The community will maintain a minimum reserve of 55 kg in the lake. Before setting out each fisher will record the number of fish they intend to keep, use a net with size gates to exclude fish below 20 cm, and weigh the catch to ensure it does not exceed 15 kg. All catches will be logged in a communal ledger; if a fisher exceeds the limit or takes undersized fish, the excess must be returned and the fisher will pay a 1 kg fine into the community pot for sustainability education. The Lake Steward Committee will enforce any temporary fishing moratorium, and the ledger keeper will collect and hold the fines. The 55 kg reserve will be monitored by quarterly fish counts, and if the lake’s stock falls below that threshold, a temporary fishing moratorium will be enacted until the reserve is restored.

agent_2.question: What is the composition and membership selection process of the Lake Steward Committee?
agent_2.answer:
The Lake Steward Committee will be made up of five members: three fishers who have consistently followed sustainable practices and have a record of keeping to the 15 kg limit, one community liaison who represents non-fisher stakeholders (such as families, local businesses, and environmental groups), and one neutral observer appointed from a local environmental agency or university to bring an objective scientific perspective.  

Selection will be by a simple majority vote of the fishing community at the quarterly gathering.  All fishers can nominate themselves or others; nominations are open for one week and then a vote is held.  Each member serves a one‑year term with no more than two consecutive terms to keep the committee fresh and responsive.  New members are inducted by the outgoing committee to ensure continuity.  

The committee meets monthly to review the quarterly fish counts, enforce moratoria if the reserve falls below 55 kg, and oversee the ledger keeper.  It also chairs the Fish Count Subcommittee and works with the Lake Steward Committee to set any temporary moratoria and to decide on fines and education spending.

agent_3.question: What happens if the lake’s fish stock falls below the 200kg minimum, and how is that violation enforced or remedied?
agent_3.answer:
If the stock falls below 200 kg, the council will call a meeting, declare a temporary fishing moratorium, and suspend all trip permits until the inventory shows the stock is back at or above 200 kg. During that time, fishermen will not be allowed to fish and must deposit any fish they already have into the communal holding bin. We will also set up a restitution fund—each fisher who helped bring the stock below the threshold will pay a fee that goes into a restocking effort. The council will decide on a recovery plan (such as restocking or reducing future quotas) and will lift the ban only when the monthly inventory confirms the minimum stock again.

The community’s rule is that if the lake’s fish stock ever dips below 200 kg, fishing stops entirely, permits are suspended, and the fishermen who contributed to the shortfall will pay restitution to help bring the stock back up. Once the stock is restored, permits are reinstated and normal fishing resumes. This keeps the lake healthy for all of us.

I will keep my own catch to myself as allowed, but I will also make sure I record my haul accurately, return any surplus to the communal dock, and pay any restitution fees if needed.

agent_3.question: How does the council determine which fishers contributed to the stock deficit and compute each fisher’s individual restitution fee when the lake’s stock falls below 200 kg?
agent_3.answer: Council looks at every fisher’s monthly log.  For each trip we note the amount of fish caught above the 2 kg limit – that is the surplus that has left the lake.  The council sums all of those surplus amounts for the month to get the total surplus.  The monthly inventory then tells us how many kilograms the lake is short of the 200 kg minimum – that’s the deficit.  Each fisher’s share of the deficit is calculated as the proportion of his or her surplus to the total surplus, multiplied by the deficit.  The fisher then pays $1 for each kilogram of that share.  Fishers who had no surplus that month pay nothing.  This proportional allocation ensures that only those who removed fish beyond the communal limit are charged for the deficit.

agent_3.question: What happens to the fish that are deposited in the communal holding bin after restitution fees are collected, and how and when are those fish returned to the lake?
agent_3.answer: The fish that we put in the communal bin are only held there as a temporary storage while the council tallies the monthly inventory and calculates how much of a deficit the lake has suffered.  As soon as the deficit has been measured and the restitution fee has been collected from each of the fishers who contributed surplus, the fish in the bin are released back into the lake in a controlled manner.  In practice that means that on the day the monthly inventory shows the lake is still below the 200‑kg threshold, the council opens the holding bin, counts the fish, and lets them swim back into the water—usually at the start of the next fishing season or immediately after the inventory so that the lake’s stock can recover.  If the inventory shows the lake has reached the 200‑kg minimum, the bin stays closed for the rest of the month and the fish are held until the next inventory round.  We do not keep the fish for longer than necessary because the purpose of the bin is to give the council time to decide how the surplus is used, and the best use is to replenish the lake.  Therefore, once restitution fees are paid, the bin is emptied into the lake on the next day of the monthly inventory, ensuring the lake’s stock is restored as quickly as possible.

agent_4.question: The proposal doesn't specify who is responsible for calculating the monthly quota from the lake’s current biomass and enforcing the return or compensation of excess fish when a fisher exceeds his quota.
agent_4.answer: I think the fair way is to have a small council of us fishers – maybe the older, more experienced ones – take on the job of measuring the lake’s biomass each month and then splitting the 10% allowance evenly. We’d keep a simple log of each trip’s haul; if someone pulls more than their share, they return the extra fish or pay a small fee to the community. The council would also check the logs to make sure no one is over the limit. That way the rule stays simple but we have a clear, trusted system to calculate and enforce the quota.
agent_4.revised_policy: Each fisher may not exceed a quota of 10% of the lake’s current biomass in any given fishing season. The community council (formed by experienced fishers) will calculate the lake’s current biomass monthly, set the 10% quota, and distribute the quota evenly among all active fishers. If a fisher’s haul exceeds his quota, he must return the excess fish to the lake or compensate the community with an agreed fee. The council will review and adjust quotas quarterly based on lake regeneration rates.

agent_4.question: The proposal doesn't specify which member(s) of the council is responsible for measuring the lake’s biomass each month and how that measurement is verified.
agent_4.answer: In my view, the responsibility for measuring the lake’s biomass each month should fall to a single, designated council member who is trained in simple sampling methods, and his results should be cross‑checked by a second council member and recorded in a shared ledger that every fisher can view. To verify the measurement, the council will conduct a random spot‑check every three months using the same method, and any fisher may request a recount if the numbers look off. This way we keep the process transparent, prevent any single person from manipulating the numbers, and still allow the council to act quickly. I will add these details to the policy so everyone knows who does the work and how it is checked.

agent_4.question: The proposal doesn't specify how the council enforces compliance and what penalties a fisher faces if they fail to return excess fish or pay the fee.
agent_4.answer:
We’ll keep the spirit of the proposal – fair share, transparency – but we’ll add clear enforcement.  The council will act as the regulator.  Every month after the ledger is updated, a council member will compare the recorded haul against the quota.  If a fisher’s haul shows a discrepancy, the fisher must present the catch record and a proof of return (or payment).  If the fisher fails to return the excess fish or pay the fee within ten days, the council will levy a penalty of twice the regular fee (0.20 USD/kg) and suspend that fisher’s quota for the next season.  Repeated violations (three times in two years) will result in a temporary ban from all communal fishing activities for six months and a community service obligation of 20 hours of lake maintenance.  The council will post any penalties and suspensions on the shared ledger so all fishers are aware.

By adding a graduated penalty system we ensure that the rule is respected without destroying the community’s trust.  The penalties are designed to be enough to deter overfishing while still allowing fishers to recover, and the public ledger keeps the process transparent.

agent_5.question: Who maintains and verifies the communal log where each fisher records their catch and 1 kg reserve?
agent_5.answer: The communal log is kept and verified by the community’s Fishery Keeper, a volunteer fisher elected by consensus. The Keeper records each fisher’s catch and the 1 kg reserve, double‑checks the numbers against the lake’s current mass, signs the log, and keeps a paper copy on the dock. Any discrepancies are investigated, and penalties are logged. This ensures the log remains accurate and that fish returned to the lake or community pool are properly recorded.

If a fisher exceeds the quota or fails to leave the 1 kg reserve, they must return the excess to the lake (or give it to the community pool) and will be barred from fishing for one day. All violations are logged and penalties enforced to keep the rule respected.

agent_5.question: How is the community pool tracked in the communal log, and how are fish transferred to it recorded?
agent_5.answer: The community pool is just another column in the communal log, kept separate from the lake‑mass line. Every time a fisher has to return fish—either because he exceeded the 15 % quota, because he failed to leave the 1 kg reserve, or because the council decided to redirect his haul to the pool—the amount returned is entered as a negative delta under the "Community pool (kg)" column for that day. The log entry therefore has: 1. Fisher name, 2. Date, 3. Catch weight, 4. 1 kg reserve, 5. Lake mass before, 6. Lake mass after, 7. Community pool delta, and 8. Council verification note. The pool amount is summed daily in a running total at the bottom of the log, and a separate audit line is drawn to show the cumulative fish in the pool. When fish are later taken from the pool (for communal use or community‑funded projects) the log records the date, the amount taken, and the purpose. This keeps the pool transparent and audit‑able. No other part of the rule changes – the quota, reserve, lake‑mass update and council verification remain exactly as proposed.

agent_6.question: What exactly is a one‑trip ban, and how is it enforced and recorded by the leader?
agent_6.answer: A one‑trip ban means I’m barred from going out for my next fishing trip. When the leader sees that I’ve exceeded 15 kg two or more times in four trips, they will write a note in the communal ledger next to my name that says "Banned – next trip" and tell me I can’t fish until the ban period ends. The ban is enforced by the leader making it clear that I cannot enter the lake during that one trip, and I must acknowledge the ban by signing the ledger. When the ban expires after that single trip, the ledger entry is cleared and I’m free to fish again.

agent_6.question: How does the leader decide whether to impose a one‑trip ban or a re‑education session for a fisher who repeatedly exceeds the 15 kg limit?
agent_6.answer: The leader looks at the ledger and counts how many times a fisher has taken more than 15 kg in any four‑trip window. For the first time that occurs, the leader writes ‘Banned – next trip’ and the fisher must skip one trip. It’s a mix of a short penalty for the first breach and a learning step for repeated or serious over‑harvests.

agent_6.question: How is the monthly rotation of the community leader determined and executed, and what process ensures that a new leader takes over the ledger and enforcement duties each month?
agent_6.answer: The rotation is a simple, predictable hand‑off that the whole crew knows. Every month we hold a quick meeting – usually right after we finish the last trip of the month – and we agree on the next person to take the chair. The order is the same as the fishing order that the crew follows each week: the person who went out first on the first week of the month becomes the leader for the next month, the next person in that order takes over after them, and so on. When the month ends the current leader does the following: 1) writes his name and the month‑ending date in the ledger header, 2) signs the last entry, 3) passes the ledger to the next fisher, and 4) hands over a written note saying “New Leader for next month: [Name].” 5) The new leader opens the ledger, reads the last entry, writes his own name and the month‑starting date in the header, and then begins reviewing entries and enforcing the rules from that point. Because everyone sees the ledger hand‑off and everyone is on the same schedule, there is no ambiguity about who has the authority to ban or call a re‑education session. That’s the process that keeps the enforcement duties cleanly passed from one person to the next each month.

5. **Loan Provision**: If a fisher’s next catch is insufficient to bring their reserve to 1 kg, the entire catch is shared, the shortfall is carried forward, and a small fish loan is granted equal to the deficit needed to reach 1 kg (capped at 1 kg). The loan is recorded in the ledger. The borrower must repay in equal installments over up to three consecutive fishing seasons, with each installment no more than half of the fisher’s catch that season after preserving a 1 kg reserve. Shortfalls are carried forward.
6. **Suspension**: First non‑compliance results in a 30‑day suspension; second consecutive offence triggers a 60‑day suspension. The committee records the suspension, informs the fisher, and prohibits any logbook entry until the suspension is lifted upon proof of compliance.
7. **Transparency**: All ledger entries—catch, quotas, fines, loans, repayments, suspensions—are kept in the shared logbook and made visible to every fisher at each meeting. This ensures accountability and allows each fisher to monitor their own reserve status at any time.

agent_5.policy: No fisher may take more than 10 % of the lake’s current stock per trip and must keep a 1 kg personal reserve for sustenance.
agent_5.operationalization: Before each trip the group meets to estimate the lake’s current stock via a designated lake‑watcher who samples and scales or, if no watcher, by consensus averaging. The 10 % limit is calculated from that estimate. Each fisher records the weight of their catch in the shared log. The lake‑watcher (or a random fisher if no watcher) verifies each catch against the 10 % limit immediately after the trip; if exceeded, the excess is logged as "Excess returned" and must be returned before the next trip. The fisher’s 1 kg reserve is weighed by the watcher before departure and logged as "Reserve kept: 1 kg – verified by [watcher]"; any shortfall forces the fisher to sit out the next trip. Excess catch from non‑compliant fishers is redistributed by a quick vote of compliant fishers after each trip, giving each an equal share. Every three months the community compares the latest lake estimate to the previous one; a change >20 % triggers a rule review, and a simple majority vote decides whether to tighten or relax the 10 % limit. Non‑compliance results in the fisher sitting out the next trip, and their excess fish is given to compliant fishers per the vote.
agent_5.reasoning: This version consolidates all clarifications: clear estimation method, transparent verification, enforceable log entries, fair redistribution, periodic review, and clear consequences, ensuring the policy is practical, democratic, and protects the lake’s sustainability while respecting individual livelihoods.

agent_6.policy: Each fisher may take no more than 12 kg per trip and the daily catch may not exceed 200 kg; exceeding the 12 kg per trip requires returning excess to the lake before leaving, and once the daily total reaches 200 kg all fishing stops until the next day; violations trigger a one‑day permit suspension, repeat violations a permanent ban.
agent_6.operationalization: After each trip, the fisher records the catch weight in the community log and signs it. The log keeper—appointed by the weekly community meeting—tallies the total, verifies that no fisher exceeded 12 kg, requests return of excess, and announces when 200 kg is reached to halt fishing. The log keeper logs any breaches; the weekly meeting reviews logs, imposes the one‑day suspension or permanent ban as stipulated, and may adjust the 200 kg cap or re‑appoint the log keeper. Fish caught beyond 12 kg must be returned to the lake before the fisher departs; failure to do so is recorded as a violation.
agent_6.reasoning: This version keeps individual limits clear, protects the lake’s daily stock, provides a transparent record‑keeping and enforcement process that builds on existing community meetings, and ties penalties directly to the log keeper’s documentation for fair, consistent enforcement.

agent_7.policy: Each fisher may take up to 10 kg per trip, and no more than 30 % of the lake’s remaining stock may be removed in a single calendar‑day round; excess must be returned within 24 h, with proportional forfeiture of next‑trip quota and possible suspension.
agent_7.operationalization: All trips are logged at the lake’s weigh‑station with a digital timestamp. A round is the 24‑hour period from 00:00:00 to 23:59:59 of a calendar day. Fishers submit a weight slip before 23:59:59; slips entered after that are logged with the next day’s date. At 00:00:00 the council sums total catch; if it exceeds 30 % of the lake’s stock at the start of the day, the excess must be returned within 24 h by the fisher who took it, verified by re‑weighing at the same station. The fisher’s share of the excess is calculated proportionally to their individual catch, and that amount is subtracted from their 10 kg standard quota for the following round, recorded in the council ledger. The ledger and a public leaderboard are updated immediately; spot‑checks are randomly scheduled throughout the day and applied only to slips recorded before the round boundary. Violations trigger a council review and may result in a one‑round suspension.
agent_7.reasoning: This version consolidates all prior discussions into a clear, enforceable policy that limits individual and collective harvests, ensures timely return of excess catch, and applies proportional penalties and suspensions to maintain fairness and lake sustainability.

agent_8.policy: Each fisher may take at most 8 % of the lake’s current fish stock per trip; 10 % of every catch is deposited into a communal emergency reserve; each fisher must keep at least 1 kg for sustenance; all catches and reserves are recorded and enforced by the ledger keeper.
agent_8.operationalization: Before each trip, the fisher reports the lake’s current stock and intended catch to the ledger keeper.  If a fisher fails to report, the keeper assumes an intended catch of 8 % of the current stock and adds a 1 kg fine to the reserve.  After the trip, the fisher reports the actual catch.  The keeper records the catch, calculates a 10 % reserve contribution, and updates the lake stock by subtracting the actual catch.  The keeper checks that the fisher’s retained catch (actual minus 10 % reserve) is at least 1 kg; if it is less, the fisher must return the shortfall or pay an equal fine.  If the actual catch exceeds 8 % of the current stock, the excess is released immediately, a fine equal to the excess is added to the reserve, and the keeper records this.  All entries, the updated lake stock, reserve balance, and any fines are posted to the public board after each round.  The communal emergency reserve is stored in a sealed tank at the dock, custodied by the ledger keeper; access is granted only to fishers on the reserve board.  The ledger keeper is elected by a simple majority of active fishers at the start of each season, serves a one‑year term, and can be replaced at a quarterly review.  Quarterly, the community reviews the lake stock and reserve balance and votes to adjust the 8 % limit if needed.
agent_8.reasoning: This version consolidates the 8 % limit, 10 % reserve, sustenance minimum, reporting obligations, fine structure, ledger keeper duties, election process, and reserve storage into a single, enforceable framework that protects both individual survival and the lake’s long‑term health.

agent_9.policy: No individual may take more than 12 kg per trip; excess must be returned to the community pool.
agent_9.operationalization: After each trip, the fisher reports the total weight to the overseer (currently Kai). The overseer posts the catch on the shared ledger. If the total exceeds 12 kg, the overseer records the surplus in the communal pool ledger entry. Daily logs are signed by the fisher and posted; the overseer verifies each log against the ledger. Any discrepancy is flagged and the fisher may challenge it; unresolved discrepancies are audited by the council. Reserves are tracked daily as cumulative catch minus any pool receipts, displayed on the ledger, and fishers with reserves below 5 kg are eligible for weekly pool distribution. Each eligible fisher may receive up to 3 kg of pool fish; priority is given to those with the lowest reserves. Allocation is decided by a simple majority vote (most votes wins) with each fisher one vote. The chair tallies the votes, distributes the fish, and records the allocation in the ledger. Failure to return excess catch results in a 2 kg fine from the next haul and possible confiscation of the excess.
agent_9.reasoning: This version consolidates the 12‑kg limit, ledger maintenance, verification, weekly distribution, priority criteria, voting rule, and penalties into a single coherent policy that the community can adopt.

agent_1.question: What constitutes a fisher’s personal reserve, and how is that reserve tracked and monitored?
agent_1.answer:
Personal reserve is the amount of fish I keep after each trip—those that sit in my own storage, on my boat or in my home—meant for my own consumption or future sale. It is the inventory I have on hand, not the fish that remain in the lake. I track it by keeping a personal ledger that records every trip’s catch, the amount returned to the lake, and the net fish I retain. The community ledger also shows each fisher’s total catch and any excess that was returned, so the reserve can be inferred by subtracting returned fish from the catch. When I exceed 8 kg in a single trip, the surplus is automatically put back into the lake, and my personal ledger marks that trip as a violation. I am barred from the next trip until my reserve falls below 5 kg; I keep the reserve at that level by monitoring my own storage and by reporting my reserve at the monthly community meeting. The community also verifies the reserve by checking the logged amounts and, if necessary, a quick visual check of my fish storage.

This system ensures everyone can see how much fish each fisher actually holds, keeps the lake’s stock in check, and gives a clear, enforceable rule for when a fisher must sit out a trip.

agent_2.answer: If a fisher fails to drop the required 25 % of their catch into the reserve, or if they go out fishing while the community has officially suspended fishing, the community will treat it as a violation of the agreement. If the fisherman repeats a violation, the community may suspend his fishing rights for a longer period (one week) or, in extreme cases, revoke his right to fish altogether until a community consensus is reached.  These measures are recorded and verified by the designated verifier to keep a transparent audit trail.

agent_4.question: Who calculates the lake’s biomass each month and assigns the 8% quotas to each fisher?
agent_4.answer: The lake’s biomass each month will be calculated and quotas assigned by the community fishery committee – a rotating group of fishermen who use the shared catch data to estimate the lake’s current biomass. The committee will publish the quotas each month in the logbook.

agent_4.question: Who receives the redistributed excess catch from a fisher who exceeds their quota, and how is that distribution determined?

The split is proportional to the unused portion of each compliant fisher’s quota: a fisher who used, say, only 5 % of his allowed 8 % gets a larger share of the redistributed fish than one who used 7 %.  This ensures that those who follow the rule are rewarded fairly for their restraint.

agent_5.question: How does the group estimate the lake’s current stock before each trip, who is responsible for making that estimate, and what method or data is used to produce the estimate?
agent_5.answer:
We’ll call a ‘lake‑watcher’ for each trip – a fisherman who’s agreed to take a quick, small‑scale sample before we head out. He/she casts a short net (or uses a baited trap) for a fixed amount of time, counts the fish caught, and notes the net’s dimensions. Using the lake’s known surface area, the watcher scales that sample to estimate total stock. The watcher’s estimate is shared with the group, entered into the shared log, and everyone agrees on it as the basis for the 10 % limit. If the watcher is absent, the group does a quick consensus estimate: each fisher gives a rough guess of how many kilos are in the lake; we take the arithmetic mean as the provisional stock. In both cases the method relies on simple sampling or consensus, both of which are transparent and easy to redo each trip.

The watcher is chosen by a quick vote or by rotating responsibility among the community, so everyone gets a turn and no single person can skew the estimate. This keeps the estimation fair and the process democratic.

Once we have the estimate, each fisher calculates 10 % of that number; that’s the maximum they may take. We still keep a 1 kg personal reserve. Excess catch is returned or redistributed as you outlined.

This doesn’t change the core of the proposal, just clarifies who makes the estimate and how.

agent_7.question: If multiple fishers contribute to exceeding the 30 % limit, how is the excess catch attributed to a specific fisher for the purpose of returning it and forfeiting the next trip’s quota?
agent_7.answer: If we all add up to more than the 30 % cap, the council will split the excess in the same ratio that each of us took the fish.  So if I took 8 kg out of a 200 kg round, and the lake started with 700 kg, I’d be responsible for 8/200 of the excess to be returned and for losing that same fraction of my next‑round quota.  That way nobody gets hit for someone else’s mistake, and we all keep our livelihoods safe.

agent_7.question: How does the council record and enforce each fisher’s forfeited share of the next‑trip quota?
agent_7.answer:
The council keeps a simple ledger that records, for every fisher, the exact amount of quota that was forfeited for the next round. When a round ends, the council computes the excess and each fisher’s share of that excess. That share is immediately subtracted from the fisher’s standard 10 kg quota and the new quota is written into the ledger for the next round.  On the day a fisher heads out, the council or a designated spot‑checker checks the ledger entry.  If the fisher attempts to take more than the recorded quota, that is a breach, and the council may suspend the fisher for one round.  The ledger is also linked to the public leaderboard so everyone can see the updated quotas and the penalties that have been applied.  In short, the forfeited share is enforced by pre‑deducting it from the next‑trip quota in the ledger and requiring the fisher to abide by that lower limit before each trip.

We then adjust the community’s shared logbook by recording the forfeiture and the reduced quota.  Spot‑checks randomly confirm that the fisher’s actual catch does not exceed the recorded quota. agent_9.question: Which existing institutional action will hold the communal pool, how will it be verified and distributed, and how are fishers' reserves defined and tracked for prioritizing distribution?
agent_9.answer: The communal pool is kept as a ledger on the shared board, with a designated keeper (currently Kai) overseeing the entries. Each fisher logs their catch weight after a trip; any portion that exceeds the 10kg limit is immediately entered as surplus in the communal pool. Verification comes from cross‑checking the posted weights: if a fisher claims 12kg, the board will show 10kg retained and 2kg added to the pool. Weekly, the pool is distributed to fishers whose personal reserves fall below 5kg. Reserves are defined as a fisher’s cumulative catch minus any fish received from the pool; they are updated on the board each day. The community prioritises distribution by lowest reserve first, ensuring the most depleted fishers receive the share. All transactions are recorded on the board, allowing anyone to audit the pool and the individual reserves at any time.
